SKL Map · Journey

1What this page is for
The map of all of SKL: the individual's journey from Point A (E0) to Ambassador (E13), the transition cells between states, and every need that moves the individual forward, in production, conversion, support and at the meta level, with their means, memories and tools.
2The principles of the map
- One model, several views. Journey, Events, Build order, Simulator and Model read the same data. Nothing is entered twice.
- The need comes first. Every card is a need. AI agents, humans and systems are means attached to the need.
- Gaps are computed. Coverage, complete cells, contracts and agent sheets are computed by rules, never entered by hand.
- Base model plus overlay. Model v5 is fixed; every change the team makes is stored on top of it and can be undone or restored.
3How to use it
- Pick the reading at the top left: Needs, Means or Fully AI target.
- Drag to move; Ctrl or ⌘ + wheel to zoom; 0 to fit all. The minimap at the bottom right is a shortcut.
- Click a card: everything not linked to it fades and its detail opens on the right, where everything can be edited.
- Filters (F key): lanes, links, coverage, add a need or a tool, jump straight to an act or a lane.
- Search (/ key); Undo at the bottom left or Ctrl/⌘ + Z.

page_methods.MechOS:
Page method
Operating System mechanism
×
1What this page is for
This page models SKL OS as two mechanisms, one per clock, built with the same Iteration system as Pre-call. Execution steering (daily, owner Romain) turns task and decision alerts into closed alerts and decisions taken. Results steering (weekly, owner Amin) turns KR readings into plans kept or changed, and sends recovery actions back to execution. Switch between them at the top right. Each model uses 21 organs spread across 5 functions (frame, matter, machinery, control, epistemic). From that model the page computes the stocks and flows, checks 5 gates, and lists the frictions that should become decisions.
2How it makes everyone more efficient
- You act on causes, not symptoms. The diagnosis points to the organ that limits the result, so effort goes to the one lever that matters.
- No iteration on a broken model. The gates stop you from testing a lever while the model leaks units or corrects faster than the system can answer.
- Facts are separated from hunches. Every value carries its evidence level, so nobody defends a guess with the confidence of a measurement.
- One shared picture. Anyone can read how the mechanism works, who owns which lever and what is deliberately left out.
3How to use it
- Build: follow the steps to construct the mechanism, one organ at a time.
- Model: read the graph left to right. Click a node to edit it; the bar on top holds what frames the mechanism.
- Organs: the 21 organs by function, each with its explanation and filling rules.
- Control: the gates, the ignorance map and the notifications. Fix what blocks first, then open a decision.
- After each test, update the organs it changed: the model improves with every cycle.
Got it

page_methods.Registers:
Page method
Registers
×
1What this page is for
Registers hold what several mechanisms share: the interfaces where one mechanism hands units to the next, the resources they compete for, the events that break comparisons, and the people who own the levers. A mechanism sheet describes one mechanism; a register describes what sits between them.
2How it makes everyone more efficient
- No orphan leaks. If Pre-call sends 61 shows and Sales counts 90 bookings, the Interfaces register shows the gap nobody owns.
- Hidden contention becomes visible. Two mechanisms that slow down together often share a saturated resource with no arrow between them.
- Honest comparisons. The Events register tells you which before/after comparison is no longer valid.
- The real human bottleneck. The Owners register shows how many levers depend on the same two or three people.
3How to use it
- Pick a register with the four tabs at the top.
- Read the four boxes: what the register holds, what it detects, how it filters iterations and when to fill it in.
- Settle the highlighted lines first: they are open questions written as TO ARBITRATE, CONFIRM or FILL IN.
- Watch the Resources load bars: a resource past its alert threshold blocks any iteration that adds volume.
- Log an event the day it happens: it takes thirty seconds and saves a wrong conclusion.
- Click a mechanism name to open its model in the Knowledge System.

Alertes et notifications

1À quoi sert cette page
C’est ici que se règle le système d’alertes. Chaque alerte surveille une condition, par exemple une tâche en retard, un résultat clé qui passe au rouge ou une décision qui dépasse son échéance. Pour chaque alerte, vous choisissez le seuil, la gravité, qui est prévenu et par quel canal. Les règles d’envoi décident quand les notifications arrivent et ce qui se passe quand personne ne réagit.
2En quoi elle rend chacun plus efficace
- Le système prévient, personne n’a à vérifier. Un écart arrive à la bonne personne au moment où il se produit, pas à la réunion suivante.
- La bonne personne, pas tout le monde. Chaque alerte va d’abord au responsable. Romain ne reçoit que ce qui a besoin de lui, ou ce que personne n’a traité à temps.
- Pas de bruit. La gravité, les heures calmes et le résumé quotidien évitent que des alertes peu utiles interrompent le travail de fond.
- Des règles qui suivent votre façon de travailler. Les seuils reprennent les règles de travail (tâches de 8 h, 3 tâches en cours, décisions en 48 h) et s’ajustent à mesure que l’équipe progresse.
3Comment l’utiliser
- Activez ou désactivez une alerte avec l’interrupteur de sa ligne.
- Cliquez sur le nom de l’alerte pour ouvrir ses réglages.
- Dans la fenêtre, ajustez le seuil avec − et +, par exemple le nombre d’heures après la date d’engagement à partir duquel une tâche est en retard.
- Choisissez la gravité (les alertes de gravité basse vont dans le résumé quotidien), qui est prévenu et les canaux. Le cadre foncé montre exactement ce qui sera envoyé.
- Réglez les règles d’envoi : heures calmes, résumé quotidien et délai d’escalade.
- Enregistrez. Revoyez les réglages à chaque planification trimestrielle : une alerte sur laquelle personne n’agit doit être ajustée ou désactivée.

page_methods.Build:
Build
What it is for
Turn a key result into a roadmap that holds: milestones anyone can check, tasks small enough to finish, estimates corrected by real records, a week that fits 54 h per person, then execution one task at a time.
The method, and where it comes from
 - Week by week: each week sets up to three milestones, results that must be true on Sunday; later weeks are built when they come.
 - Milestones are results, checked on Sunday 8 pm against proof lines (OKR practice: outcomes, not activities).
 - Definition of ready and done for tasks: a verb, a done-when, one owner, 4 h at most.
 - Reference-class forecasting and calibration: estimates are compared with similar past work and corrected by each person's actual ÷ estimated record.
 - Priority by due date and critical path: the task of the earliest milestone goes first, then the one that unblocks the most.
 - Pre-mortem: assume failure, list the causes, mitigate them before starting.
 - Daily planning: each day starts with three objectives (results visible tonight) and a timed roadmap that fits the focus hours; it is validated before the first task.
 - Work in progress = 1 in Execute: one card at a time, the day's timeline above it, the real time recorded.
 - End-of-day review: what is not finished is replanned on the spot (tomorrow first, back to the queue, or dropped) with what got in the way; the EOD recap is then written from the day and posted to Slack once you validate it.
Decisions taken for SKL OS
 - Task: 4 h at most; above that it is split.
 - Milestone: a result with proof lines; 3 per week at most, only this week's are required, and a fourth one must be chosen out before going further.
 - Priority is computed by the OS. A person cannot reorder the queue; a lead can override with a written reason.
 - Planned work: 9 h a day, 6 days a week (54 h). Help given to colleagues comes on top and is counted per person.
 - Each person commits their own roadmap of the week, with no blocking issue on their milestones and tasks; it opens Execute for them.
 - Help requests wait until the current card is done, unless marked urgent; their cost on your milestone is shown. Every answer (accept, later today, tomorrow, decline) sends a message to the person who asked, prepared for that answer or written by Claude from your main points.
 - Blocked needs a reason and who it waits on; it raises a risk on the milestone.
 - The Cockpit is unchanged; it reads the plan, the actual times and the help given.
How to use it
- Pick a key result, then go through the six steps on the left; red marks show which rule is broken.
- Ask Claude at each step. Every suggestion shows a preview and a reason; nothing changes until you accept it.
- Commit, then open Execute.
 Coefficients are measured from Execute (actual ÷ estimated, last four weeks); until four weeks exist they come from the Registers (config "coefficients"), 1.3 by default. Plans, weeks, days and requests are shared through SKL OS.
